name: Novice fundamentals
description: Your first two or three months, before any of it needs to work against resistance: how to be safe, how to move, and a map of where you are. Everything here completes from showing up and drilling — no live rounds required — so it finishes while a belt roadmap is just getting started.

phases.title: Being a good training partner
phases.description: Nothing in jiu-jitsu is worth an injury — yours or theirs. This is the material every good academy teaches first, and the only part of the sport you are expected to be good at on day one.

items.title: Tap early, tap often
items.notes: A tap is information, not defeat: it says the position was lost ten seconds ago and you now know why. Tap physically on their body, tap loud, and say it if your hands are trapped. Recognise your partner's taps the same way — verbal, physical, or a stopped struggle.

items.title: Protect the people you train with
items.notes: Control your body weight, put submissions on slowly, and let go the moment they tap. Know what is off-limits for beginners at your academy — typically heel hooks, neck cranks and slams — and keep it off-limits even when one is offered to you.

items.title: Mat etiquette
items.notes: Clean gi, short nails, no shoes on the mat, shoes everywhere else. Tell the coach about skin problems before they become the whole academy's problem. Start rounds on time, don't coach mid-roll, and assume everyone is having a harder week than you.

phases.title: The movements under everything
phases.description: Every escape and every sweep is built out of half a dozen movements. Drill them until they stop costing attention — the criteria here count classes drilled, not wins, because a movement pattern is earned by repetition across weeks, not by one good night.

items.notes: Falling is the first skill: chin tucked, arms slapping, never a hand posted behind you.
The fall you actually take from most throws. Same rule: the mat takes the impact, not your wrist.
Over the shoulder, not the head — the roll that turns being pushed into repositioning.
The hip power behind every mount escape. Heels close, bridge to a shoulder, not straight up.
The one way to stand up that doesn't give your legs away while you do it.
Hips down and back the moment someone shoots — the difference between defending a takedown and reacting to one.
Base, balance and posture while moving. Everything standing starts from here.

phases.title: The map
phases.description: Jiu-jitsu makes no sense as a list of moves and complete sense as a map of positions. Learn the map first: where you are, what it is worth, and which way is up.

items.title: The positional hierarchy
items.notes: From best to worst for the person in control: back control, mount, knee-on-belly, side control, north–south, half guard, guard, turtle, standing. Every roll is both people trying to climb this ladder at once — most of what looks like chaos is just two climbs colliding.

items.title: Top and bottom are different games
items.notes: On top you pass, pin and attack; on the bottom you frame, escape and recover guard. Guard is the one bottom position that is not losing — your legs are between you and them, and that is a weapon.

items.title: Position before submission
items.notes: The oldest rule in the sport and the one under every other. Control where the fight is before you spend anything on a finish — a submission attempted from a bad position usually costs the position and lands nothing.

items.title: Connection, frames and inside position
items.notes: Frames are bones placed where their weight wants to go — a forearm at the neck, an elbow inside a knee. Inside position means your arms and knees are between their limbs, not around them. Whoever owns the inside owns what happens next.

phases.title: Survive first
phases.description: Before anything can be attacked, the bad places have to stop being emergencies. Drill the survival postures until being pinned is merely uncomfortable — the escapes themselves belong to the white belt roadmap; this is the part that keeps you safe while you learn them.

items.title: The defensive sequence
items.notes: In order, always: protect your neck, bring your elbows in, build frames, restore your alignment, make space, recover guard or get on top. Skipping ahead — reaching for an escape before the neck and elbows are safe — is how survivable positions become submissions.
Elbows connected to knees, hands guarding your neck. Mount stops being terrifying the day this becomes automatic.
A forearm at the neck and a frame at the hip. You are not escaping yet — you are making their pin cost something.
Chin down, hands win the fight over your collar. Losing your back is a position lost, not a round lost — as long as your neck stays yours.

name: White belt: survive and escape
description: The white belt question is: where am I, and how do I survive or improve my position? This roadmap works through it in the order it actually goes wrong — get out of the bad places first, then stop losing the guard you have, then the handful of attacks that genuinely work at white belt. Milestones complete from what you log live; the concepts around them are the ideas each phase is really teaching.

phases.title: How this belt works
phases.description: White belt is roughly 40% escapes and defense, 20% guard retention, 20% positional control, and only 10% submissions — and that split is the curriculum, not a limitation of it. A white belt who can survive, escape and hold position is dangerous at blue; one who only hunts submissions is starting over.

items.title: Defense is the syllabus, not the warm-up
items.notes: Protect the neck, then the elbows, then frame, then move. Every phase below starts from the bottom of its position on purpose: you will spend most of this year underneath people, and what you do there decides how fast the rest arrives.

items.title: Know when the escape is gone
items.notes: Armbar straight and your elbow past their hips: tap. Choke sunk under the chin: tap. The skill of recognising a lost position early is worth more this year than any single escape — it is what lets you roll again tomorrow.

phases.title: Mount: get out, then hold
phases.description: The worst place a beginner spends time, and the first thing worth fixing. The expectation by the end: escape mount against training partners of comparable experience, hold it for short stretches without just being heavy, and connect two attacks from the top.

items.title: The elbow–knee connection
items.notes: Elbows tight to knees is what makes every mount escape possible and high mount impossible. The moment an elbow floats away from your body, it belongs to them.
When someone mounts you and reaches for something, you can put them underneath you.
The escape that works when they don't give you the roll: elbow, knee, half guard, guard.

items.title: Holding mount is hips, not weight
items.notes: Grapevines, a low base, hands posting against the bridge — and climbing to high mount when they turn on their side. Chasing submissions before the mount is stable is how you end up back in their guard.
Holding the pin is not the end of the round — the arm they use to push is the arm you take.

phases.title: Side control: frames before everything
phases.description: Where every passed guard lands and every stalled roll settles. Bottom first — being pinned is uncomfortable rather than dangerous, and you can keep it that way — then the top game: a pass is not finished until side control is stabilised.

items.notes: Being pinned is uncomfortable rather than dangerous, and you can keep it that way.
You can turn frames into space and get your guard back.

items.title: Protect the near arm
items.notes: Most of what goes wrong under side control starts with the near arm drifting — into a crossface, an americana, an arm triangle. Elbow to your ribs, hand guarding your neck, always.
What you passed to, you keep.
The far arm is an attack that starts from the pin you already hold.

phases.title: Closed guard: your first weapon system
phases.description: The one bottom position that attacks. The expectation by the end: break posture on demand, two sweeps that work, one sweep connected to one submission, and an opening game from the top that doesn't feed your arms to an armbar.

items.notes: Nobody stands up and opens your guard on their terms.
You can sweep from closed guard and end up on top.
When they sit back to open your guard, the space they made is the sweep.

items.title: The attacks arrive together
items.notes: Triangle, armbar and omoplata are one system with three exits — defending one exposes the next. Learn the triangle first, then notice the armbar is already there every time they pull the arm out.
When they leave an arm in and posture up, the triangle is already there.
A closed guard does not stop you: you can open it standing and cut straight through.

phases.title: Half guard is a position, not a failure
phases.description: Half guard is where passes stall and where bottom players start winning exchanges. Recognise it as a real position with its own battle — the underhook — rather than a guard that half-failed.

items.title: The underhook battle decides everything
items.notes: Bottom half guard with the underhook is an attacking position; bottom half guard flattened under a crossface is mount with extra steps. The knee shield buys the time; the underhook spends it.
The frame that stops the crossface arriving and keeps the distance yours.
Underhook, up to the knees, and their base is suddenly negotiable.
From the top, half guard is a pass that is already half done: crossface, flatten, free the knee.

phases.title: Open guard: keep it, pass it
phases.description: White belts do not need every open guard — they need retention that survives pressure, one sweep from distance, and passing that starts from control instead of from hope.

items.title: Four points of contact
items.notes: An open guard is alive while your feet and hands are connected to them — feet on hips, grips on sleeves or collar. Lose the connections and you are not playing guard, you are lying down near an opponent.
When someone starts to pass, you can move your hips and take your guard back.
A standing opponent has two legs and you have grips on both — the floor does the rest.

items.title: Pass from headquarters, not from anywhere
items.notes: One position — their bottom leg controlled between yours — feeds the knee cut, the toreando and the smash. Passing from a named place beats improvising around flying feet.
Their legs are steering wheels: move them, not yourself, and walk around what's left.

phases.title: The back: escape it, take it, finish from it
phases.description: The top of the positional hierarchy, in both directions. The expectation: hands that defend your neck automatically, one reliable escape, and a rear naked choke that finishes when the back is yours.

items.notes: Losing your back costs you position, not the round.
Fall toward their choking arm, shoulders to the mat, and walk out the side door.
The finish the whole hierarchy points at. Position first, seatbelt kept, and the choke arrives on its own.

phases.title: Turtle: a door, not a home
phases.description: Turtle is a position you move through — to guard, to your feet — never one you wait in. Staying still in turtle is volunteering your back.

items.title: Elbows and knees closed, neck hidden
items.notes: A safe turtle has no gaps: elbows connected to knees, chin down, hands denying the collar. Every hook and every choke starts through a gap you left open.
From turtle you are one sit-out from having your guard back — take it before they take your back.

phases.title: Standing: how rounds begin
phases.description: Every match and most rolls start here. The expectation is modest and real: one takedown you can finish, one you can stop, and the habit of getting back to your feet safely.

items.notes: When the round starts standing, you have a way in.
When the shot isn't there, chest to chest and a trip is.
Their best shot ends with your hips on their shoulders.

phases.title: The graduation standard
phases.description: What this roadmap adds up to. None of it is a promotion — that is your coach's call, made on the mat — but an athlete who clears these milestones has the game a new blue belt is supposed to have.

items.title: What the record should show
items.notes: Two mount escapes and two side-control escapes that work against your peers. A back escape and a neck that defends itself. Two sweeps, a sweep connected to a submission, and a guard you can open and pass three ways. Two takedowns and a sprawl. Positions held, not just reached.

items.title: What it deliberately leaves out
items.notes: Leg locks beyond knowing when to tap, berimbolos, and everything your favourite competitor does on Saturday. Blue belt is where a game gets built — this year is for the base it gets built on.

name: Blue belt: building a game
description: The blue belt question is: how do I reliably attack from every major position? You already know how to survive — this belt is about choosing where the fight happens: one guard you play on purpose, one pass you trust, attacks that connect to each other instead of arriving one at a time, and the first honest look at the front headlock and the legs.

phases.title: How this belt works
phases.description: Blue belt is where a game starts being chosen rather than inherited. Four questions run through everything below: what is my preferred game, what reactions am I trying to create, what is my second attack when the first fails, and how do I get back to my strongest position?

items.title: Systems, not moves
items.notes: A technique you know is a fact; a technique connected to the opponent's likeliest defence is a system. Every phase below pairs a first attack with where it sends you when it fails — that pairing, not the move list, is what blue belt adds.

phases.title: Defensive consolidation
phases.description: White belt escaped the ordinary pins. Blue closes the gaps: technical mount, the body triangle threat, late-stage submission defence — the escapes that work after the easy window has closed.

items.notes: Having your back taken stops being the end of the round.
The arm is under your chin and you still get out.
Technical mount is where trap-and-roll goes to die — this is the escape that lives there.

items.title: Defend late, not just early
items.notes: Every submission has an early, middle and late stage, and white belt only taught the early one. The middle is hand fighting; the late is structure — and knowing which stage you are in decides whether you fight or tap.

phases.title: Guard retention: the layers
phases.description: Retention is a ladder you fall down in order: distance, foot frames, knee frames, hand frames, hip movement, inversion, late recovery. A guard is hard to pass when losing one layer just means arriving at the next.

items.notes: Your legs get back in front of them before they can settle into the pass.

items.title: Retention is posture, not scrambling
items.notes: Feet between you and them, knees inside their lines, hands on the outside. When retention feels like panic it has already failed — the work happened two layers earlier.

phases.title: Closed guard: the chain
phases.description: At white belt the closed-guard attacks were separate answers. Now they are one question asked three ways: the defence to each attack is the entry to the next.

items.notes: One trapped arm gives you three finishes, and their defence to each one opens the next.
The kimura grip is a fork: they post, you finish; they tuck, you sweep. Either answer is yours.

phases.title: Half guard: from surviving to winning
phases.description: White belt made half guard a real position. Blue makes it profitable — the underhook battle won on purpose, and a second engine underneath when the first stalls.

items.notes: Half guard stops being where you get stuck and becomes where you get on top.
When the underhook is contested, the hook under their thigh is the tiebreaker.

phases.title: Two guards that answer each other
phases.description: Not every open guard — two that cover each other's failures. The pairing here is De La Riva at long range and butterfly at close range; if your academy plays a different pair, the principle is the pairing, not these guards.

items.notes: You have a guard you go to on purpose, not the one you end up in.
When they stand up to pass, you take them down instead.
When they kneel and hug close, the hooks lift what their base was standing on.
Butterfly is also a doorway: elevate, slide under, and arrive at their leg with your whole body.

phases.title: Passing: one pressure, one movement
phases.description: A passing system needs a fast answer and a heavy answer, and they share a structure: control the feet or knees, set the angle, defeat the frames, control the hips, then the shoulders, then stabilise. A pass that skips a step is a scramble wearing a name.

items.notes: You pass from one place you know, instead of improvising every time.
You have a pass you trust, and a ready answer for the way people stop it.
A knee in your chest stops being the end of your passing.
The heavy answer: chest to chest, their hips pinned, and nothing for their guard to hold onto.

phases.title: Pins that go somewhere
phases.description: Blue-belt pins are dynamic: side control, knee-on-belly, north–south and mount are one position seen from four angles, and the submissions live in the transitions between them.

items.notes: When they turn away from the pin, you are already behind them.
Once you have the back you keep it, without racing for a finish.
You can finish from the back against someone who knows exactly what is coming.
The pin they think is a rest stop has a choke in it.

items.title: A failed submission should end somewhere better
items.notes: Attack so that the worst case is an improved pin — an armbar that loses the arm but keeps mount, a choke that converts to a back take. If failing costs the position, the attack was priced wrong.

phases.title: The front headlock
phases.description: Every snapdown, every stuffed shot and every duck-out lands here, and at blue belt it stops being a place where you just hold a neck. Chin strap and elbow control first — the chokes only work from a headlock that already controls them.

items.notes: The arm-in headlock is already most of a darce — learn to see the choke that is nearly finished.

items.title: Position before choke, here too
items.notes: Chin strap, elbow blocked, their head below your chest. Go behind when they defend the neck, choke when they defend the go-behind — the headlock is a fork, not a squeeze.

phases.title: Legs, responsibly
phases.description: Leg locks start with positional responsibility, not with submissions: control the position, know the rule set, and protect your training partners. The straight ankle is the whole family in miniature — everything harder is this with higher stakes.

items.notes: Single-leg X is first a sweep: their base goes, you come up, and the leg is still there if you want it.
The first leg attack, finished with the hips, released early. How you treat this one decides what you may be taught next.

items.title: Defensive responsibility in entanglements
items.notes: Control their second leg, clear your knee line, hide the heel, stand up through the gap. And the one that matters most: rotational pressure on a knee is a tap, not a puzzle — at every belt.

phases.title: Standing: chains, not singles
phases.description: One takedown fails against anyone good. Blue belt wrestling is the second attempt arriving before the first one has finished failing — and the takedown flowing straight into the pass.

items.notes: You can start the match on your feet and finish the exchange on top.

items.title: Chain the shot to the finish, and the finish to the pass
items.notes: Snapdown sets up the single, the single converts to the double, the double lands already past the guard. A takedown that ends standing still in their guard scored two points and started a new problem.

phases.title: The graduation standard
phases.description: What this roadmap adds up to — and as always, promotion is your coach's call, made on the mat, not a progress bar.

items.title: What the record should show
items.notes: Reliable escapes from every major pin. Two guards that answer each other, with retention underneath both. One pressure pass and one movement pass. Submission chains from mount, side control, back and guard — chains, not singles. A front headlock that forks, basic leg-lock literacy, and wrestling that comes in sequences.

name: Purple belt: connections
description: The purple belt question is: how do I connect attacks and force predictable reactions? Purple is less about new moves than about joining up the ones you already have — a personal game named out loud, one guard taken from entry all the way to the back, one pass taken all the way to its counter, and the kimura and the legs as systems rather than submissions.

phases.title: Name your game
phases.description: Purple belt starts with an architecture, written down: a primary standing entry, a primary guard, a secondary guard that solves the primary's problems, a passing system, and a finishing system. The phases below build one such game — swap the pieces for yours, but have answers for every slot.

items.title: A-game, B-game, emergency game
items.notes: The A-game is what you impose; the B-game is where you go when they refuse it; the emergency game is what happens when you are losing. Purple belt is knowing which one you are in — and moving between them on purpose rather than on panic.

items.title: Techniques become decision trees
items.notes: Every attack below is recorded with its counter and its counter's counter. If you cannot say what they will do when your sweep fails, you do not have a sweep — you have a hope with grips.

phases.title: Retention under everything
phases.description: Advanced retention is retention against intent: against leg drags, body locks, floating passers, and your own fatigue. Inversion joins the ladder, and turtle stops being a defeat and becomes a transitional guard.

items.notes: Your guard is hard to pass because you can turn upside down and still find their legs.
Turtle stops being somewhere you wait and becomes somewhere you leave.
Locked legs around your waist are a problem you solve, not one you survive.

phases.title: One guard, all the way down
phases.description: A developed guard is an entry system, a retention system, sweeps, back takes, wrestle-ups and leg entries that all start from the same grips. Here that guard is the K-guard; the shape of the phase is what matters, whatever your guard is.

items.notes: You can leave closed guard on your terms instead of waiting to be opened.
You get up and get on top from underneath, without giving up the leg.
When they defend the sweep, you end up behind them instead.
The same grips also enter the legs — the guard's fourth answer, for the opponent who has learned the first three.

phases.title: The back takes underneath
phases.description: Purple belt guard play points at the back: berimbolo and the crab-ride family turn a defended sweep into an arrival behind them. Expensive to learn, and worth it — the back is the one destination nobody concedes on purpose.

items.notes: When they hide the far leg from your sweep, invert under and come up on their back instead.
Deep half is the b-side of the same idea: disappear under their base and surface on top.

phases.title: The kimura trap
phases.description: At purple the kimura stops being a shoulder lock and becomes a control system: a grip that passes guards, takes backs and survives scrambles, with the finish as just one of its exits.

items.notes: Their half guard holds your leg; the kimura holds something they need more.
When they turn away from the grip, the grip goes with them — and you arrive on the back holding it.

phases.title: Float passing, and the reaction map
phases.description: Advanced passing reads reactions instead of forcing outcomes: weight on their knees, direction changes off their answers, and a map of where each defence sends you next.

items.notes: You pass by staying light on top rather than by out-muscling their guard.
When the float gets read, you change direction instead of restarting.

phases.title: Pins, backs, and the dilemmas between them
phases.description: Advanced control is making every escape attempt cost something: the pin follows them instead of resisting them, and each defensive turn exposes the next attack.

items.notes: Once you take the back, they stay there while you work.
Their own defensive hand becomes the thing that finishes them.
Turning in to escape your pass becomes the mistake that ends the round.

phases.title: The front headlock system
phases.description: Blue belt found the darce. Purple owns the whole junction: arm-in and arm-out, chokes that trade with go-behinds, and the headlock as the answer to every failed shot — theirs and yours.

items.notes: Someone locking a guillotine on your neck is a problem you solve, not a tap.
When they defend the darce by staying tight, the necktie was the price of staying tight.

phases.title: Leg entanglements as positions
phases.description: Purple treats entanglements the way white treated pins: positions with controls, escapes and exchanges — not lotteries. Sweep from them, pass from them, and defend them with structure instead of luck.

items.notes: You know the saddle when you are in it, and you tap early rather than test your knee against it.
Hide the heel, control the line, and leave through the door their control left open — calmly, before the rotation starts.
50/50 is only symmetrical on paper: whoever off-balances first is playing it alone.

phases.title: Scrambles, owned
phases.description: A scramble is not chaos — it is a race with rules: hips lower than theirs, head on the winning side, and a known exit. Purple belts finish takedowns against real sprawls and come up from turtle attacking.

items.notes: You finish the single you already have, even against a good whizzer.
From turtle you do not just recover guard — you come up attacking their legs.

phases.title: Tactics, and the standard
phases.description: Purple belt is the first belt with a scoreboard brain: pace, score, boundaries, when to stabilise and when to scramble, how to protect a lead and how to chase one. And as at every belt: promotion is your coach’s call, made on the mat, never a progress bar.

items.title: Manage the round, not just the exchange
items.notes: Know the score, know the clock, and know which of your games the situation calls for. Winning positions with thirty seconds left and losing ones with three minutes left are different sports.

items.title: What the record should show
items.notes: A recognisable personal game, named and drilled. Positions that connect without pausing. Reactions you created on purpose, and second attacks that were waiting for them. Entanglements entered and survived. And the ability to explain why — to a training partner, out loud.

name: Brown belt: one game, no leaks
description: The brown belt question is: how do I impose, adapt, refine, and teach a complete game? Almost nothing here is new — it is material you have had for years, held to a standard nobody applies at blue. A third of it is scored on attacks that never land on you rather than on ones you hit, and the rest is a single connected game where every escape ends in an attack.

phases.title: What brown belt is
phases.description: Refinement, not accumulation. The goal is not more techniques — it is proven techniques made extremely difficult to stop: timing, weight, grip efficiency, energy conservation, and control kept through every transition.

items.title: The defensive chain, complete
items.notes: Prevent the position, prevent the control, prevent the isolation, prevent the alignment, clear the submission, recover the position, counterattack. Brown belt defence works so early it looks like nothing happened.

phases.title: The pins stop working on you
phases.description: Escapes held to the brown-belt standard: out before the control settles, out against specialists, and out into an attack rather than into a reset.

items.notes: Purple made the body triangle solvable; brown means you are out before their hands finish.
Being mounted ends with you attacking a leg, not with you back in guard.
The escape you learned in your first month, now working more often than it fails.

phases.title: The submissions stop landing
phases.description: The room’s best attacks, scored on facing them and stopping them. A defended count is evidence that the attack arrived and failed — which is the only version of safety that can be logged honestly.

items.notes: You learned the early escape at white and the late one at blue — now the strangle simply does not land.
At white you learned to land this; at brown nobody lands it on you.
Turning in to get out stops being the thing that gets you strangled.
At purple you knew the saddle and tapped early — now you get the leg back instead.
The most common pass in the room does not work on you.
At white this was your way in; now it is simply that nobody gets in on you.

phases.title: Elite retention
phases.description: Retention against every passing family, with limited grips, under explosion and under grind — and the deliberate choice of turtle over a compromised guard, made calmly.

items.notes: Nothing gets past your knee, and it has not for a long time.

phases.title: One connected game
phases.description: The A-game as a single circuit: the pass chains into the back take, the back cycles through mount and comes back, and prolonged control is a way to win — not a failure to finish.

items.notes: You do not have a pass — you have a sequence, and it does not stop when the first one fails.
The leg drag stops ending in side control and starts ending behind them.
Purple kept the back through their first escape; brown keeps it through their best one.
When they slip the back they slip into mount, never into your guard.

items.title: Move around frames, never through them
items.notes: Control the hips and shoulders, remove the wedges, follow their escapes into better controls. Forcing through a frame spends strength to stay even; moving around it spends nothing and gains ground.

phases.title: Submission families, finished
phases.description: Brown belt submissions are families with shared mechanics — isolate, control the rotation, control the next joint, remove slack, finish progressively. The legs join as a full family where the rule set allows.

items.notes: The outside heel hook, from the position that makes it safe to hold and quick to release — control first, and let go the moment it is answered.

phases.title: Standing, specialised
phases.description: A primary takedown family, a complement, a counter system, and the mat return — the standing game as one structure rather than a list of throws.

items.notes: When they stand up out of your control, they come back down still in it.

phases.title: Strategy, troubleshooting, teaching
phases.description: The parts of brown belt that happen between rounds: match plans, score and energy management, diagnosing a failing technique, and the leadership the belt quietly obligates.

items.title: Diagnose before you drill
items.notes: A failing technique fails for a reason from a short list: distance, connection, angle, a missing control point, weight in the wrong place, timing, or the wrong reaction read. Name the reason first — drilling a mis-diagnosed technique rehearses the mistake.

items.title: Adapt it to the body it belongs to
items.notes: Modify for body type, age, flexibility, injury and rule set — yours and your students'. Knowing the difference between personal preference and universal principle is most of what teaching is.

items.title: Teach a beginner safely
items.notes: Structure a class, match partners sensibly, explain the positional goal before the technique, and correct without overwhelming. A brown belt is what most white belts think a black belt is — act accordingly.

phases.title: The graduation standard
phases.description: The record a brown belt approaching black should show — and, one last time: promotion is your coach's call, made on the mat.

items.title: What the record should show
items.notes: No major positional weakness. A highly developed A-game with supporting systems. The room's best attacks failing against you at a rate you can point to. Varied guards passed, scrambles owned, leg-lock literacy appropriate to the academy — and juniors who are measurably better because you train with them.
